area: Area X. Slow Flight, Stalls, and Spins
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain spins at commercial-pilot depth, enter and recover from an intentional spin in an approved airplane while you explain it, and teach spin awareness: plan a safe spin lesson, demonstrate it, and spot and fix the common errors.
why: A spin needs only a stall plus yaw, and mishandling the controls in turns, stalls and uncoordinated slow flight can put even a reluctant modern airplane into one [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Most stall/spin accidents came from distraction in routine flight, not from intentional practice [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Flight instructor airplane and glider applicants are the only pilots required to receive spin training, with a logbook endorsement, in an aircraft certificated for spins [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]] [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300]].

warmup: Think first: a CFI applicant you are training holds full right rudder and full back elevator, the airplane breaks into a right spin, and after half a turn they freeze with both inputs still in. You are 5,600 ft AGL in an airplane approved for spins. What do you say, what do you do with your hands and feet, and in what order? Now flip it: on the ground before that flight, which three things would you have checked about the airplane itself to be sure the recovery will work?

key_terms.def: An aggravated stall that results in autorotation, with the airplane following a downward corkscrew path [[13:11|AC 61-67C 107]].
The self-sustaining rotation of a spin: the rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing, giving rolling, yawing and pitching [[13:11|AC 61-67C 107]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C 107]].
The phase in which the pilot, on purpose or by accident, provides the elements for the spin: a stall plus yaw [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
From the stall and start of rotation until the spin is fully developed; aerodynamic and inertial forces are not yet balanced [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
Rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed are stabilized in a nearly vertical flightpath; the spin is in equilibrium [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
Rotation ceases and the wing's AOA drops below the critical AOA; it may last a quarter turn to several turns [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
A spin with near-level pitch and roll attitude and the spin axis near the CG. Recovery may be extremely difficult or impossible [[13:13|AC 61-67C 110c]].
A descending turn in which the airplane is not stalled, so airspeed and G-load can increase rapidly [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

The logbook endorsement a CFI airplane or glider applicant needs, showing competence and instructional proficiency in stall awareness, spin entry, spins and spin recovery [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]] [[12:49|AC 61-65K A.49]].
A parachute made under a type certificate or a TSO (C-23 series), or an identified military personnel parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].
An illusion after a proper spin recovery of spinning the other way; the disoriented pilot puts the airplane back into the original spin [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]].
Application: the recovery control inputs, mainly brisk full opposite rudder and forward elevator, with ailerons neutral and power idle [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

chunks.title: Purpose: spin awareness for all, spins for instructors

body.p: Spin awareness means two things every pilot needs: being proficient at avoiding the conditions that lead to an accidental stall/spin, and promptly taking the correct actions to recover to normal flight [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Upon recognition of a spin or an approaching spin, the pilot should immediately execute the spin recovery procedure [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

Spin training is different. The flight training required by Part 61 does not include actual spins for anyone other than flight instructor airplane and flight instructor glider applicants; for everyone else it emphasizes stall and spin avoidance [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]]. Spin training is required for those instructor applicants only [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300]].

Why the instructor needs it: incipient spins are practiced to train the instructor applicant to recover from a student's poorly performed stall or unusual attitude that could lead to a spin [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300d]]. Practicing full stalls with learners can result in inadvertent spins [[25:191|AIH 10-7]], so the person in the right seat must be able to stop one.
Procedures, in outline (each step is taught later in this lesson). The AC 61-67C plan for instructor applicants [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300]]:

bullets: 1. Use an aircraft approved for spins and consult the AFM or POH for the proper entry and recovery [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300a]].
2. Begin with power-on and power-off stalls to learn the aircraft's stall characteristics [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]].
3. Practice spin avoidance, incipient spins, spin entry, spins and spin recovery from above 3,500 ft AGL [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]].
4. The instructor demonstrates spin entry, spin and recovery; the applicant repeats them in both directions [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]].
5. The instructor who gave the training endorses the applicant's logbook or training record [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300]].

callout.text: CFI ACS note for this Task: at the evaluator's discretion, a logbook record attesting your instructional competency in spin entries, spins and spin recoveries may be accepted in lieu of this Task, certified by the flight instructor who gave the spin instruction. Appendix 2 adds that the applicant and the instructor or evaluator must always recognize and avoid operations that could lead to an inadvertent stall or spin.

Application: say the two words apart from the first lesson. 'Spin awareness' is every pilot's job on every flight; 'spin training' is a planned flight in an approved airplane. Learners who mix them up either fear every stall or treat placarded airplanes as spinnable.

check.q: Which pilots does AC 61-67C say practice actual spins as part of the training Part 61 requires?
check.a: Only flight instructor airplane and flight instructor glider applicants; for others the training emphasizes stall and spin avoidance [[13:15|AC 61-67C 200]] [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300]].

chunks.title: The CFI spin rule, the endorsement and parachutes

body.p: The rule is 14 CFR 61.183(i). For a flight instructor certificate with an airplane or glider rating, the applicant must receive a logbook endorsement from an authorized instructor that they are competent and possess instructional proficiency in stall awareness, spin entry, spins and spin recovery procedures, after flight training in those areas in an airplane or glider certificated for spins [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]].

The applicant must also demonstrate instructional proficiency in those areas. An examiner may accept the endorsement as evidence for the practical test, unless the test is a retest after a failure for deficiencies in stall awareness or spin instruction; then the examiner must test the person in an airplane or glider certificated for spins [[60:340|14 CFR 61.183(i)(2)]]. A failed applicant must get more training and an endorsement, bring an aircraft certificated for spins to the retest, and demonstrate to the examiner [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(b)]].

bullets: Who needs it: every flight instructor airplane applicant, even one who first seeks a flight instructor certificate with an airplane multiengine rating [[12:21|AC 61-65K 26.1]].

The endorsement: AC 61-65K gives a sample that names 61.183(i), says airplane or glider, and states the person is 'competent and possess[es] instructional proficiency' in the four areas [[12:49|AC 61-65K A.49]].
Who signs: the flight instructor who provided the training [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300]].

body.p: Parachutes. 14 CFR 91.307 has three parts you will use as a spin instructor:

head: Rule
What it says
Source
rows: Packing
A parachute carried for emergency use must be an approved type, packed by a certificated and appropriately rated rigger within 180 days (synthetic fibers) or 60 days (any natural fiber)
Limits
With any person aboard other than a crewmember, no intentional maneuver past 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose-up or nose-down unless each occupant wears an approved parachute
Exception

The limit does not apply to flight tests for pilot certification, or to spins and other maneuvers required by the regulations for any certificate or rating when given by a CFI (or an ATP instructing under 61.67)
CFI spin training
Spins are required for the flight instructor airplane rating, so neither the person receiving the instruction nor the instructor giving it must wear a parachute

callout.text: Read 91.307(d) exactly: it lifts paragraph (c) only for flight tests for a pilot certificate or rating, and for spins and other flight maneuvers required by the regulations for a certificate or rating when given by a CFI or by an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]]. Application: a spin ride for a pilot who is not training for a certificate or rating that requires spins fits neither, so paragraph (c) governs it. Then, with any person aboard who is not a crewmember, no maneuver may exceed 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees nose-up or nose-down unless each occupant wears an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]. The AFH also tells you to review the current Part 91 parachute requirements before any spin [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

check.q: Under 14 CFR 91.307(d), who may give required spin instruction for the parachute exception to apply?
check.a: A certificated flight instructor, or an airline transport pilot instructing in accordance with 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]].

chunks.title: Spin aerodynamics: the relationships the ACS names

body.p: A spin is an aggravated stall that results in autorotation. As the airplane rotates around a vertical axis, the rising wing is less stalled than the descending wing, which creates a rolling, yawing and pitching motion, and the airplane is forced downward by gravity in a spiral path [[13:11|AC 61-67C 107]] [[13:12|AC 61-67C 107]]. Teach each K2 relationship as a row:

head: Factor
What it does in a spin
Source
rows: Angle of attack
All spins are preceded by a stall on at least part of the wing; in all spins at least one wing is stalled, and the descending wing is at the greater AOA
Airspeed
Low and constant in a spin, because the airplane is stalled; if it is increasing, the airplane is no longer in a spin
Load factor
Usually only slightly above 1 G in the spin, since airspeed is very low and the airplane pivots rather than turns; about 2.5 G in a proper recovery
Power setting
Power aggravates spin characteristics: it can flatten the spin attitude and usually increases the rotation rate
Airplane weight and CG
Minor weight or balance changes affect spin characteristics; an extremely aft CG can lead to a flat spin, and recovery from a flat spin is often impossible
Airplane attitude
Normally nose low on a downward corkscrew path; a flat spin has near-level pitch and roll with the spin axis near the CG
Yaw effects
Rudder misuse, adverse yaw from aileron, P-factor, torque, spiraling slipstream, gyroscopic precession, wind shear and wake turbulence can all yaw the airplane at the stall

body.p: CG, in more depth. An airplane that recovers cleanly from a prolonged spin at one CG may fail to respond to normal recovery when the CG moves aft by one or two inches, which is why the aft CG limit for utility-category spins is usually several inches forward of the normal-category limit [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]]. In a flat spin, centrifugal force acting through an aft CG pulls the tail out from the spin axis so the nose cannot be lowered [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]. A forward CG has its own trap: many airplanes will not spin at forward CG locations but will spiral [[13:13|AC 61-67C 112]].

Various configurations. If the flaps or retractable gear are extended before the spin, retract them as soon as practicable after spin entry [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Under the older normal-category spin test, flaps extended could be retracted during recovery but not before the rotation had ceased [[13:21|AC 61-67C 400a]]. Application: those two lines differ in timing, so for your airplane the POH decides; teach spins only in the configuration it approves.

callout.text: Application: draw Figure 5-16's two wings on a whiteboard, with one relative-wind arrow each. Ask the learner which wing has more drag and which way the airplane will yaw. When they see that the more-stalled wing drags back and down, autorotation stops being a mystery.

check.q: Why does an airplane that is loaded within its normal-category CG range still worry you on a spin flight?
check.a: Spin recovery is very sensitive to CG: moving it aft one or two inches can stop a normal recovery [[1:140|PHAK 5-43]], and an extremely aft CG can lead to a flat spin that is often unrecoverable [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]]. Spins may be approved only at the more restricted utility loading [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

chunks.title: What causes a spin, and the four phases

body.p: Cause. A spin occurs when at least one wing exceeds the critical AOA with a sideslip or yaw acting on the airplane at or beyond the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. The primary cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the critical AOA while applying excessive or insufficient rudder and, to a lesser extent, aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]]. A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can spin in the direction of the rudder, regardless of which wingtip is raised [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

head: Phase
What is happening
How to identify it
rows: Entry
The pilot, on purpose or by accident, provides the elements for the spin [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Stall plus yaw. If the yaw came from wrong rudder, the pilot may not know the critical AOA was exceeded until the airplane yaws out of control toward the lowering wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]
Incipient
From the stall and start of rotation until the spin is fully developed; forces not yet balanced; may take two to four turns for most airplanes [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]

Indicated airspeed generally settles low and constant, and the turn indicator shows the spin direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Figure 5-16 gives about 4 to 6 seconds and about 2 turns in light aircraft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]
Developed
Rotation rate, airspeed and vertical speed stabilized in a nearly vertical path; aerodynamic and inertial forces in balance [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Attitude and motions constant or repetitive from turn to turn [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]; small trainers lose about 500 ft per 3-second turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]
Recovery
Rotation ceases and the AOA drops below the critical AOA; a quarter turn to several turns [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Rotation stops and the wings regain lift; trainers usually recover about a quarter to half a turn after anti-spin inputs [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]

body.p: The look-alike. Some training airplanes will not enter the developed phase and can instead transition unexpectedly from the incipient phase into a spiral dive, which is not in equilibrium: it accelerates and the G-load can rise rapidly [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. A spiral is recognized by rapidly increasing airspeed after the attempted spin entry; in an actual spin the airspeed normally stabilizes [[13:20|AC 61-67C 300f]].

callout.text: Application: on spin flights, have the learner call the phase out loud: 'stall, rotation, incipient', then 'stable' or 'speed rising'. Calling 'speed rising' trains the spiral recognition that matters as much as the spin itself.

check.q: Your applicant expects the spin to be fully developed after one turn. What does the AFH say about the incipient phase, and when do you start an incipient spin recovery?
check.a: The incipient phase may take two to four turns in most airplanes, and incipient spin recovery should start before 360 degrees of rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

chunks.title: Is this airplane approved for spins?

body.p: The first rule for spin demonstration is to ensure the airplane is approved for spins [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. If the manufacturer does not specifically approve an aircraft for spins, intentional spins are not authorized by the CFRs [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. The official sources [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]:

bullets: Type Certificate Data Sheets or the aircraft specifications.
The limitations section of the FAA-approved AFM/POH, including limits on gross weight, CG range or fuel. The POH flight limits list prohibited maneuvers such as spins [[1:234|PHAK 9-4]].
A placard in clear view of the pilot, for example 'NO ACROBATIC MANEUVERS INCLUDING SPINS APPROVED'.

body.p: Airworthiness category. A standard airworthiness certificate is issued for aircraft type certificated in the normal, utility, acrobatic, commuter or transport category [[24:24|AFH 1-3]]. AC 61-67C describes how the older Part 23 rules treated spins in each category:

head: Category
Spin standard (older Part 23, per AC 61-67C)
Placard
rows: Normal
Not approved for spins; tested only to recover from a one-turn or 3-second spin in one more turn, so behavior beyond that is unknown [[13:21|AC 61-67C 400a]]
'No acrobatic maneuvers, including spins, approved' [[13:22|AC 61-67C 401a]]
Utility
If approved for spins, meets the normal and acrobatic spin requirements [[13:22|AC 61-67C 400c]]
Lists approved maneuvers and entry speeds; 'Spins Prohibited' if it does not meet the acrobatic spin requirements [[13:22|AC 61-67C 401]]
Acrobatic
Recovers from any point up to six turns in no more than one and a half more turns [[13:21|AC 61-67C 400b]]
Lists approved maneuvers, entry speeds and the spin recovery control actions [[13:22|AC 61-67C 401]]

body.p: Current rule. Today 14 CFR 23.2150 requires airplanes certified for aerobatics that include spins to recover within one and one-half additional turns from any point in a spin, up to six turns or more if certification is requested; single-engine airplanes not certified for aerobatics must not tend to depart controlled flight inadvertently [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. The older one-turn standard still applies to airplanes certified under it [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

Weight and balance decide approval on the day. An airplane approved for spins in the utility category but loaded in the normal category may not recover from a spin that goes beyond one turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Extra weight in the aft baggage compartment or extra fuel can stay inside the CG envelope and still seriously affect spin recovery [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]; in one two-place airplane no baggage may be carried aft of the seats when spins are practiced [[1:139|PHAK 5-42]].

callout.text: In airplanes placarded against spins there is absolutely no assurance that recovery from a fully developed spin is possible, and some pilots and even instructors have ignored placards, calling them a technicality [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Assume a placarded airplane may become uncontrollable in a spin [[13:22|AC 61-67C 402]].

check.q: Your trainer is approved for spins in the utility category. Today you will have full fuel and a bag in the back. What do you check before you spin?
check.a: That the actual weight and CG are within the utility category limits in the AFM/POH, because loaded in the normal category it may not recover beyond one turn, and aft weight or extra fuel can hurt recovery even inside the envelope [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

chunks.title: Unintentional spins: where they start and how to see them coming

body.p: Flight situations where unintentional spins may occur (K7) and the factors behind them (R1). The cross-control setup at base to final is taught in depth in the cross-controlled stall lesson (AI.X.F); here is the wider list:

head: Situation
Why it can end in a spin
Source
rows: Base to final overshoot
The pilot tries to rudder the airplane around (skid) rather than overshoot or steepen the bank
Go-around or short-field takeoff
High pitch, high power, low airspeed: too little or too much rudder for P-factor gives uncoordinated flight at a high AOA
Gliding steep turn after an engine failure
Rudder pushed toward the bank while pulling to hold altitude can rapidly become an unrecoverable spin
Uncoordinated flight near the ground
Holding uncoordinated control deflections creates the potential for a spin, especially in the traffic pattern
A botched stall recovery
An improper recovery can lead to a secondary stall or a spin
Distraction
Tasks secondary to flying raise the risk of an inadvertent stall or spin; 60 percent of stall/spin accidents occurred during takeoff and landing, and 20 percent followed an engine failure
Autopilot disconnect
A sudden self-disconnect with controls trimmed into uncoordinated flight can lead to a spin or spiral

body.p: Recognize conditions that lead to a spin for future avoidance (K10). An airplane must be stalled and yawed to spin, so continued practice in stall recognition and recovery builds a more instinctive reaction to an approaching spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Teach the learner to look for the two ingredients together: a high AOA (slow, nose high, pulling, or a steep turn) plus yaw (ball out, rudder held, power changing). Keeping the nose from yawing before the stall recovery starts is the key to averting a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Modern airplanes are more reluctant to spin, but not immune [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
Range and limitations of stall warning indicators (R2), as they bear on spins:

bullets: Masked by the skid: in an uncoordinated maneuver the pitot-static instruments, especially the altimeter and airspeed indicator, are unreliable, so the pilot may not know the critical AOA is near until the stall warning device activates [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].
Small margin: many warning devices alert only 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].
Failure: a stall warning system can fail; then buffet, loss of roll authority or an inability to arrest a descent must warn you [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Contamination: in some icing the stall comes with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]].
Testing: stall warning devices should not be deactivated for flight tests in airplanes that require them [[13:22|AC 61-67C 402]].

callout.text: The rudder decides the spin direction in a cross-controlled stall, not the raised wing [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. A learner who expects the airplane to roll the 'obvious' way will be surprised; tell them before the first stall demonstration.

check.q: Your learner climbs on autopilot with the ball well out and the airplane trimmed that way. Why does AC 61-67C worry about this setup near a stall?
check.a: A sudden autopilot self-disconnect with the controls trimmed into uncoordinated flight complicates the post-stall recovery and may lead to a spin or spiral; the autopilot can also mask some stall cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102c]].

chunks.title: Intentional spins: entry, minimum altitude and a stabilized spin

body.p: Entry procedure (K8). The entry for demonstrating a spin is similar to a power-off stall [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]:

bullets: 1. Slowly reduce power to idle while raising the nose to a pitch attitude that ensures a stall [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Handle the throttle with care and use carburetor heat as the manufacturer recommends [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].
2. As the airplane approaches the stall, smoothly apply full rudder in the direction of the desired spin and full back elevator to the limit of travel [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
3. Keep the ailerons neutral unless the AFM/POH says otherwise [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

body.p: Minimum entry altitude (K8, S2). The sources give three numbers; plan to the highest that applies:

head: Source
Altitude
What it governs
rows: AFH
Begin high enough to complete recovery at or above 1,500 ft AGL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]
Any intentional spin
Practice spin avoidance, incipient spins, spins and recovery from above 3,500 ft AGL [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]]
CFI spin training
CFI ACS
"Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 4,000 feet AGL." (AI.X.I.S2)
Your checkride

body.p: Altitude loss: the first turn loses about 1,000 ft and each later turn about half that [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. AC 61-67C's rough estimate is about 500 ft per 3-second turn in most small airplanes approved for spins, with greater losses at higher density altitude [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. So the entry altitude is the highest terrain plus 4,000 ft plus the turns you plan, plus the recovery.

Control procedure to maintain a stabilized spin (K9). Application from the entry and the template: hold what started it. Full rudder in the spin direction and full back elevator to the stop [[24:129|AFH 5-24]], ailerons neutral, power at idle, since power flattens the spin and speeds the rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Not holding full up-elevator during entry gives a spiral instead [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. In the AC training plan the spin is allowed to develop and is fully recovered no later than one full turn, with an eye on the airspeed indicator so it never reaches the red line [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]].

callout.text: S3, exactly: "Enter and recover from an intentional spin if requested by the evaluator." The evaluator may instead accept a certified logbook record (Task note), and 61.183(i)(2) lets an examiner accept the spin endorsement unless it is a retest for spin deficiencies [[60:340|14 CFR 61.183(i)(2)]]. Arrive ready to fly it, in an airplane approved for spins.

Application: on the entry, say each input as you make it: 'idle, nose up, full left rudder now, stick full back, ailerons neutral.' The learner hears the order and you hear yourself keep the ailerons out of it.

check.q: Highest terrain in the practice area is 1,800 ft MSL. You plan a one-turn spin. Using the AFH loss figure, what is the lowest entry that meets the ACS?
check.a: 1,800 + 4,000 (ACS floor) + 1,000 (first turn) = 6,800 ft MSL, and higher in practice to allow for the recovery [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] (AI.X.I.S2).

chunks.title: Orientation: which instruments tell you the spin direction

body.p: Orientation during a spin (K11). Application: outside, the ground is turning quickly, so teach the learner to get the spin direction from the instruments the AFH names:

head: Instrument
Use in a spin
Source
rows: Turn indicator (turn coordinator symbolic airplane or turn needle)
Reliable: shows the direction of the spin, and a deflection in the direction of rotation if you are disoriented
Slip/skid ball (inclinometer)
Not reliable for direction: its mounting location decides how it moves; a ball on the left side of the airplane moves left even in a right spin
Airspeed indicator
Low and constant in a spin; if it is increasing, you are not in a spin

body.p: How the turn coordinator works: its gimbal is canted, so the gyro senses both rate of roll and rate of turn, and it shows only the rate and direction of turn, not a bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]].

Disorientation (R6). After a proper recovery from a spin that has stopped stimulating the inner ear, the pilot can feel a spin in the opposite direction and put the airplane back into the original spin: the graveyard spin [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. An abrupt head movement in a prolonged turn can create the Coriolis illusion of rotation on another axis [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]; keep head movements small [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Pilots may not know they are disoriented, and unrecognized disorientation leaves them taking no corrective action [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

callout.text: Application: before each entry, have the learner say the planned spin direction aloud, and after rotation starts have them confirm it from the turn indicator before calling the recovery rudder. 'Left spin, turn coordinator left, right rudder' builds the cross-check you want under stress.

check.q: After a left spin recovery the learner says 'now we're turning right' and starts to push left rudder, but the turn coordinator is level. What is happening?
check.a: Probably the graveyard spin illusion: after a recovery the inner ear signals a spin the other way, and the pilot may re-enter the original spin [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. Believe the turn indicator [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

chunks.title: Recovery: the manufacturer first, then the AFH template

body.p: Spin recovery procedure (K4). Follow the manufacturer's recommended procedure; use the AFH six-step template only when the manufacturer gives none [[24:129|AFH 5-24]] [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Incipient spin recovery should start before 360 degrees of rotation, with full rudder opposite the rotation [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

head: Step
Why, in the AFH's words, simplified
Source
rows: 1. Power to idle
Power aggravates the spin: flatter attitude, usually faster rotation
2. Ailerons neutral
With the spin they can speed the rotation and delay recovery; against it they can flatten the spin and may cause an unrecoverable spin
3. Full opposite rudder, held
Usually the most important control; apply it briskly and fully, since slow, cautious rudder can let the airplane keep spinning
4. Brisk forward elevator
Right after the rudder, without waiting for the rotation to stop; it lowers the AOA; some airplanes need full forward
5. Neutralize rudder
When the rotation stops; otherwise the rising airspeed gives yaw or sideslip
6. Back elevator, power as needed
Return to level flight without excessive back pressure, which can cause a secondary stall and another spin; stay inside G and airspeed limits

body.p: AC 61-67C words it a little differently: close the throttle, neutralize the ailerons, determine the direction of the turn and apply full opposite rudder; when the rotation slows, move the elevator briskly forward to about neutral (some airplanes need only relaxed back pressure, others full forward); neutralize the rudder when the spinning stops to avoid a spin in the opposite direction [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. It also warns that the engine can quit from fuel interruption in a spin, so assume power is not available when practicing recovery [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

Minimum recovery altitude (K12). The AFH wants recovery complete at or above 1,500 ft AGL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]; on the checkride the Task must be complete no lower than 4,000 ft AGL (AI.X.I.S2). The pull-out from the steep nose-low attitude brings higher airspeeds and load factors than a stall recovery [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]], typically about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

If it turns into a spiral, fly the spiral recovery instead: power to idle, some forward elevator to unload to about 1 G, roll wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder, then gently raise the nose and add climb power at VY [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

callout.text: Risk in the recovery itself (R3): each step done late, slowly or too hard creates its own hazard. Slow rudder can keep it spinning, aileron against the spin can flatten it, rudder left in after the rotation stops can start a spin the other way, and a hard pull can cause a secondary stall and another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

check.q: Why should you expect a harder pull-out after a spin recovery than after a stall recovery?
check.a: The nose is much lower at the end of a spin recovery, so the airspeed and the load factor in the pull-out are higher [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]; a proper spin recovery usually loads about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

chunks.title: Planning the lesson: airplane, traffic, weather and altitude

body.p: Before any spin flight the AFH asks for a review of the AFM/POH limitations, placards or type data for spin approval; weight and balance limits; the recommended entry and recovery; and the current Part 91 parachute rules [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. On the preflight, look hard for loose items that could shift the weight and CG, and for slack rudder or elevator cables that could prevent full anti-spin deflection [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

Collision hazards (R5) and clearing (S1). Clear the area above and below the airplane before any intentional spin; this may be done while slowing for the entry [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. Clearing procedures should precede spins; in a high-wing airplane raise the wing toward the turn and look, in a low-wing airplane lower it and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Haze and crowded practice areas aggravate the hazard, and you and the learner share the lookout [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Application: a spin drops about 1,000 ft in the first turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], so the airspace below you matters more than for any other maneuver.
Environmental elements (R4):

bullets: Turbulence: a large variation in wind over a short distance can cause an upset and loss of control [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]; wind shear and wake turbulence also yaw the airplane at the stall [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Application: postpone spin training in turbulence; you want the learner's first spins to be the airplane's normal behavior.
Microbursts: they can produce very powerful updrafts, downdrafts and roll forces [[28:265|AWH 22-10]]. Stay away from convective weather on spin days.

High density altitude: expect greater altitude loss per turn [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]; the type of spin an airplane enters can depend on density altitude [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]; and the engine makes less power [[1:166|PHAK 7-6]], so the climb back to entry altitude takes longer.

body.p: Clouds and ceilings. Do not teach at an altitude that leaves too little room to recover, such as below a cloud layer [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. If the weather will not allow the altitude, change the lesson to ground or simulator work, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

callout.text: Application: build a one-line plan on the kneeboard before engine start: highest terrain, plus 4,000 ft, plus planned turns times the AFH loss, equals minimum entry; and the cloud base you need above it. If the numbers do not fit under the clouds, it is a ground lesson today.

check.q: The forecast is a broken layer just above your planned spin entry altitude with light turbulence. What do the sources lead you to do?
check.a: Do not spin below a cloud layer that leaves too little room [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; turbulence can cause an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Change the lesson to ground or simulator work, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

body.p: Human factors associated with spin instruction (K5). Anxiety is probably the most significant psychological factor in flight instruction, and the fear of falling is universal [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. A learner terrified of spins may be unable to listen to the lesson at all, so the anxiety has to be addressed first [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]. Treat fears as normal, introduce the maneuver with care so the learner knows what to expect, review the aerodynamics, and describe the sensations and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]. Ease learners into flight regions they fear [[25:39|AIH 2-6]].

head: What you may see
Why
What you do
rows: The learner freezes, holding the spin inputs
Responses to anxiety range from hesitancy to doing something wrong; many freeze [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]
Take the controls and calmly say 'I have the flight controls'; anxious learners can be incredibly strong, and fighting them gains nothing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
A fight-or-flight reaction at the break
Stalls and spins can trigger it, leaving little time to think [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]
Break the maneuver into stages and let them practice each until comfortable [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]; incipient spins first [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Startle at the roll-off
Startle is an automatic reflex to a sudden event that violates expectations [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Brief exactly what the entry looks and feels like; later, scenario-based training with realistic distractions [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]
Nausea, paleness, sweating
Motion sickness, which is no reflection on ability [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]
Shorter flights, fresh air, eyes outside, few head movements; no motion sickness medication for the pilot [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]
Calls the wrong direction after recovery
Graveyard spin illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]
Cross-check the turn indicator [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]

body.p: Distractions, task prioritization and loss of situational awareness (R6). Most stall/spin accidents happened when attention was diverted from flying [[25:179|AIH 9-9]], which is why spin avoidance training uses realistic distractions such as dropping a pencil, reading a chart or reaching into the back seat [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300c]] [[13:16|AC 61-67C 200a(10)]]. Budgeting time and prioritizing tasks can leave enough time to finish them without error [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. In the airplane you must also keep your own picture: altitude remaining, position over the practice area and traffic below.

callout.text: Improperly delivered stall, spin and upset training often results in negative learning, with consequences that last beyond the lesson [[24:113|AFH 5-8]]. Never let a learner exceed your limits, and stay within your own ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Application: set your take-over point (a turn count or altitude) on the ground and tell the learner.

check.q: Your applicant gets pale and quiet after the second spin. What does the PHAK suggest, and what should you avoid?
check.a: Treat it as motion sickness, which says nothing about ability: open the vents, keep eyes outside, limit head movements, and use shorter flights; do not have the pilot take motion sickness medication [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

body.p: Ground first. Learning stalls goes slower through flight instruction alone than when the types and aerodynamics are discussed on the ground, and the task should be reviewed before flight even after ground school [[25:174|AIH 9-4]]. For spins, cover the four phases, the instruments, the recovery and what the learner will feel [[25:45|AIH 2-12]], and brief the positive exchange of flight controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
A building-block flight plan drawn from AC 61-67C and the AFH:

bullets: 1. Power-on and power-off stalls in the clean configuration, to learn this airplane's stall and recovery [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]].
2. Spin avoidance: stalls and slow flight with realistic distractions. Performance is unsatisfactory if the instructor must take control to avoid a fully developed spin [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300c]].

3. Incipient spins: from a power-on or power-off stall, keep the back pressure, add rudder at the stall and let the nose yaw toward the stalled wing, then release the spin inputs and recover with opposite rudder and forward elevator as the spin begins; discuss the control use [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300d]]. Incipient spins are the most commonly used maneuver in initial spin training [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].
4. The instructor demonstrates spin entry, spin and recovery; the applicant repeats them in both directions, recovering no later than one full turn [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]].
5. Spiral recognition: if a spin does not develop, show how the airspeed rises and recover at once [[13:20|AC 61-67C 300f]].

body.p: Fly it while you explain it (S3). On the checkride, narrate the clearing, the altitude check, each entry input, the phase you see, the instrument that shows the direction, and each recovery step as you make it. The ACS skills header asks you to demonstrate and simultaneously explain.

Rehearse the role. The AIH describes a CFI applicant briefing and demonstrating stalls while another instructor plays an anxious learner, followed by a critique [[25:100|AIH 4-7]]. Do that for spins with your own instructor before the checkride, and practice the take-over.

callout.text: Application: give each recovery step a callout the learner says out loud as their hand or foot moves: 'idle, neutral, rudder, forward, rudder neutral, ease out.' Use the POH's own steps if it has them. You can hear a missing step before you see it.

check.q: The evaluator, as your learner, applies full opposite rudder briskly but moves the stick only to just aft of neutral, and the rotation goes on. Which listed error is this, and what is your correction?
check.a: Failure to apply sufficient forward elevator during recovery [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Apply positive, brisk, straight-forward elevator, forward of neutral, right after the rudder; some airplanes need full forward [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. Follow the POH where it differs.

body.p: The AFH lists 10 common errors in intentional spins [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. On the checkride the evaluator may play a learner and make them; you analyze and correct (AI.X.I.S4).

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Not full rudder to the stops in the spin direction on entry [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
A wing drop or a sloppy, slow rotation instead of a clean entry
Smooth, full rudder as the stall approaches [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Not full up-elevator held on entry, giving a spiral [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Nose drops steeply and the airspeed rises
Elevator to the limit of travel and held [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Not fully stalled before the spin input [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Rudder makes a skid or a spiral, not a spin
Raise the nose to a pitch that ensures a stall first [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]
Recovery rudder not full and brisk [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Rotation continues or slows only a little
Full opposite rudder, briskly, to the stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Too little forward elevator [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Rudder in, but rotation goes on; airplane still stalled
Positive, brisk forward elevator, forward of neutral; some airplanes need full forward [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Waiting for the rotation to stop before forward elevator [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Rudder in, stick still back, turns adding up
Elevator immediately after the rudder [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Rudder not neutralized after the rotation stops [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Yaw or sideslip as speed builds, possibly a secondary spin
Rudder neutral as the rotation stops [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Slow, overly cautious control movements [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Hesitant inputs, recovery taking turns
Brisk, positive technique [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Too much back elevator after the rotation stops [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Buffet or a second break in the pull-out
Smooth back pressure; avoid a secondary stall [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]
Too little back elevator in the recovery [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]
Long dive, airspeed toward the red line
Return to level flight once rotation stops, within airspeed limits [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]]

body.p: Diagnose the cause, not just the input. Have the learner talk through the spin; you will hear whether a missing step is a misunderstanding or a motor skill problem [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]. The AIH generally prefers letting a learner go part of the way into a mistake, safety permitting [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]; in a spin the margin is altitude, so decide in the brief how far that can go.

callout.text: Application: the most useful single observation is the airspeed indicator. Rising speed on the entry points to error 2 or 3; a very low steady speed with continuing rotation after anti-spin inputs points to errors 4, 5, 6 or 8.

check.q: The evaluator, as your learner, holds full opposite rudder briskly but keeps the stick back, saying 'I'll push once it stops turning.' Which error is this and what is your correction?
check.a: Waiting for the rotation to stop before applying forward elevator, a listed error [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. Apply positive, brisk forward elevator immediately after the rudder; do not wait [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

scenario.title: A CFI applicant's spin training flight on a marginal day
scenario.setup: You are a CFI giving Maya, a commercial pilot working toward her flight instructor certificate, the training 14 CFR 61.183(i) requires. Your two-seat trainer's POH approves spins in the utility category only. The practice area's highest terrain is 1,400 ft MSL. The morning forecast has a scattered to broken layer near 7,000 ft MSL with light chop below it, and the practice area is popular with other schools. Maya slept poorly and says she is 'a bit nervous about the real spins'.

questions.q: Maya wants to put her flight bag and a full water jug behind the seats. What do you check?
questions.a: That the weight and CG stay within the utility category limits in the AFM/POH. Aft weight can seriously affect spin recovery even inside the CG range, and loaded in the normal category the airplane may not recover beyond one turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]; some two-place airplanes allow no baggage aft of the seats for spins [[1:139|PHAK 5-42]].

questions.q: She asks if you both need parachutes. You have one in the hangar, packed eight months ago. What applies?
questions.a: Required CFI spin training given by a CFI is excepted from the parachute rule [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]] [[13:20|AC 61-67C 301b]]. But a parachute carried for emergency use must have been packed within 180 days (synthetic) [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(a)]], so leave that one behind.

questions.q: Can you meet the altitude plan under the forecast layer?
questions.a: The ACS floor is 1,400 + 4,000 = 5,400 ft MSL, and a one-turn spin loses about 1,000 ft, so entry is at least 6,400 ft MSL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] (AI.X.I.S2), close to a 7,000 ft base. Do not teach below a layer that leaves too little room [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]; if the layer is lower than forecast, switch to ground work or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: The chop and the busy practice area: what do you do about them?
questions.a: Turbulence can cause upset and loss of control [[24:107|AFH 5-2]], so delay the spins until it is smooth. Clear above and below before every entry, even while slowing [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], and share the lookout with Maya [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

questions.q: After her first incipient spin recovery Maya says she does not want to try a full spin today. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Treat the fear as normal and do not force it [[25:45|AIH 2-12]]; ease her into the regime she fears [[25:39|AIH 2-6]]. Let her practice the stages, more incipient spins, until comfortable [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]; incipient spins are the most common maneuver in initial spin training [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]. Brief the full spin for the next flight.

questions.q: After a good recovery she pulls hard and feels a buffet. What happened, and how do you debrief it?
questions.a: Excessive back elevator after the rotation stops can cause a secondary stall and another spin [[24:130|AFH 5-25]], a listed common error [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]. The spin pull-out already loads about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]], which raises the stall speed; ease it out within G and airspeed limits.

skills.do: Clear the area, above and below, before the entry, explaining why a spin's large altitude loss makes the airspace below matter most.
skills.practice: Clear with full callouts while you slow for each entry, as the AFH allows [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], raising or lowering the wing to look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

skills.do: "Select an entry altitude that allows the Task to be completed no lower than 4,000 feet AGL", and say how you got it: highest terrain, plus 4,000 ft, plus the planned turns and recovery.
skills.practice: Before each training flight, write the terrain height and the AFH turn losses (about 1,000 ft for the first turn, half that for each later one) on the kneeboard and work out the entry [[24:128|AFH 5-23]].

skills.do: "Enter and recover from an intentional spin if requested by the evaluator", in an airplane approved for spins, explaining each entry input, the phase, the direction from the turn indicator and each recovery step; or present the certified logbook record the Task note allows.
skills.practice: Fly spins in both directions with your spin instructor, narrating aloud each time [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]], and recovering by the POH procedure [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors as the evaluator makes them: name the error from the AFH list, say what you saw, give the fix.
skills.practice: On the ground, drill the 10 AFH spin errors [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]; in the air, have your instructor make some on purpose and call each one with its fix.

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 61.183(i)(2), when may an examiner NOT accept your spin training endorsement in place of a demonstration?
options: When you are adding only a flight instructor multiengine rating
When the endorsing instructor did not also sign your practical test recommendation
When it is a retest after a failure for spin or stall awareness instruction
When you logged fewer than 15 hours as PIC in the category and class
quiz.why: The examiner may accept the endorsement unless the test is a retest after a failure for deficiencies in stall awareness, spin entry, spins or spin recovery instruction [[60:340|14 CFR 61.183(i)(2)]].

quiz.q: According to the PHAK, why is the load factor in a stabilized spin usually only slightly above 1 G?
options: The rotation is too slow, about 3 degrees per second, to load the wing measurably
The descending wing makes negative lift, which cancels the extra G of the turning path
Airspeed is very low, near the 1 G stall speed, and the airplane pivots rather than turns
Power is at idle, so no thrust component adds to the load carried by the wings
quiz.why: The PHAK gives two reasons: airspeed in a spin is very low, usually within 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed, and the airplane pivots rather than turns [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]].

quiz.q: During the incipient phase, what does the AFH say generally happens to the indicated airspeed?
options: It climbs steadily, since the nose points nearly straight down
It swings widely from turn to turn until the developed phase
It reads zero, since the pitot tube sits in separated airflow
It settles at a low and constant value as the phase develops
quiz.why: As the incipient phase develops, the indicated airspeed will generally stabilize at a low and constant value [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

quiz.q: A trainer is approved for spins in the utility category. If it is loaded within the normal category instead, what does the AFH warn?
options: Spins stay approved, but only to the left, away from engine torque
It may not recover from a spin allowed to go beyond one turn
It recovers normally, just with more altitude lost on each turn
It cannot spin at all, since the extra weight prevents the stall
quiz.why: An airplane approved for spins in the utility category but loaded per the normal category may not recover from a spin that progresses beyond one turn [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

quiz.q: Under the older 23.1567 placard rules that AC 61-67C quotes, what must the placard in a spin-approved utility or acrobatic airplane give besides the approved maneuvers?
options: The minimum entry altitude for spins and the loss for each turn in feet
The parachute packing dates and the name of the rigger who packed them
The spin entry speed and the number of turns the pilot is allowed to log
The spin recovery control actions and when recovery must start
quiz.why: For acrobatic airplanes and utility airplanes approved for spins, the placard lists the control actions for recovery from spinning and says recovery must start when spiral characteristics appear, or after not more than six turns or any greater number certificated [[13:22|AC 61-67C 401e]].

quiz.q: For an intentional spin entry, what does the AFH say about the ailerons?
options: Keep them neutral unless the AFM/POH says otherwise
Hold aileron against the spin to keep the bank angle from steepening
Hold aileron toward the spin direction so the rotation starts sooner
Use them freely to hold the wings level until the nose falls through
quiz.why: Unless the AFM/POH specifies otherwise, the ailerons are kept neutral during the spin procedure [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

quiz.q: In a prolonged spin your learner turns her head sharply to look at the wingtip and feels the airplane tumbling on another axis. What illusion is this?
options: The leans
The Coriolis illusion
The somatogravic illusion
The graveyard spiral
quiz.why: An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn that has stopped stimulating the motion sensing system can create the illusion of rotation on an entirely different axis: the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-6]]. Keep head movements small [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

quiz.q: What does AC 61-67C recommend you assume about engine power when practicing spin recovery, and why?
options: Assume full power, since the throttle stays open through the spin
Assume none: centrifugal force can interrupt fuel to the engine
Assume partial power, since carburetor heat lowers the output
Assume it returns after one turn, once the fuel settles again
quiz.why: The engine sometimes stops developing power because centrifugal force on the fuel interrupts the fuel supply, so assume power is not available when practicing spin recovery [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].

quiz.q: Your applicant's anxiety at each break turns into a fight-or-flight reaction. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Repeat the full maneuver many times in one flight until the fear wears off
Stop all spin training, since fight-or-flight means she is not suited to instruct
Take it apart, demonstrate each stage, and let her practice the stages
Skip the briefing so she has less time to build up worry before the maneuver
quiz.why: Fight or flight leaves little time to analyze; the instructor can take the procedure apart, demonstrate each stage, and let the learner practice the stages until comfortable [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].

quiz.q: In the AC 61-67C training plan, who demonstrates spin entry, spin and recovery, and how does the applicant then practice it?
options: The instructor demonstrates; the applicant repeats it in both directions
The applicant goes first; the instructor then repeats it to the left only
The instructor demonstrates; the applicant repeats it to the left, against torque
Neither: CFI applicants fly incipient spins only, never a full spin entry
quiz.why: Spin entry, spin and recovery should be demonstrated by the instructor and repeated in both directions by the applicant [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]].

final_quiz.q: During spin avoidance training with distractions, your applicant lets the airplane go so far that you must take the controls to stop a fully developed spin. How does AC 61-67C grade that?
options: Satisfactory, since recognizing the spin is the goal and not the recovery itself
Unsatisfactory: needing the instructor to take over to avoid it fails the task
Satisfactory if she names the error correctly in the debrief after landing
Not graded, because spin avoidance is only practiced and never evaluated
final_quiz.why: Spin avoidance training uses stalls and slow flight with realistic distractions, and performance is unsatisfactory if the instructor must take control to avoid a fully developed spin [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300c]].

final_quiz.q: An owner says his normal-category airplane was spin tested during certification, so a few turns of spin are fine for training. What do you answer?
options: Agree, if the spin is stopped within three turns, as in the certification test
Agree, if both of you wear approved parachutes, since 91.307 then allows it
Agree, if a CFI is aboard, since 91.307(d) allows any spin with an instructor
Disagree: it may have been tested only to a one-turn or 3-second spin
final_quiz.why: Normal-category airplanes certified under 23.221(a) only had to recover from a one-turn or 3-second spin; in placarded airplanes there is no assurance of recovery from a developed spin, and intentional spins are not authorized [[24:130|AFH 5-25]].

final_quiz.q: In the AC 61-67C plan for full spins with your applicant, by when should each spin be fully recovered, and what do you watch?
options: By one full turn; watch the airspeed so it never reaches VNE
By two turns; watch the altimeter so you stay above 3,500 ft AGL
By three turns; watch the turn coordinator for the spin direction
By half a turn; watch the slip/skid ball until it centers again
final_quiz.why: Allow the spin to develop and fully recover no later than one full turn, observing the airspeed indicator during the spin and recovery so it does not reach the red line (VNE) [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]].

final_quiz.q: You are writing your applicant's 61.183(i) endorsement. In which areas must it say she is competent and has instructional proficiency?
options: Stall awareness, spin entry, spins and spin recovery procedures
Incipient spins, developed spins, flat spins and spin recovery
Spin entry, spins, spiral dives and spin recovery procedures
Stall recovery, spin entry, spins, upset and spiral dive recovery
final_quiz.why: 61.183(i)(1) names stall awareness, spin entry, spins and spin recovery procedures, after training in an airplane or glider certificated for spins [[60:339|14 CFR 61.183(i)]]; the AC 61-65K sample uses the same four areas [[12:49|AC 61-65K A.49]].

final_quiz.q: Your trainer is hard to spin when loaded in the utility category. A colleague says that means it is even more spin resistant at normal-category loading. What does the AFH say?
options: He is right: the extra weight at normal loading keeps the wing from reaching the stall
He is right: normal-category loading moves the CG forward, which prevents spin entry
It is the same at either loading, because the spin approval covers both categories
It could resist spin entry less, since the farther aft CG lets it reach a higher AOA
final_quiz.why: An airplane that is difficult to spin in the utility category (restricted aft CG, less weight) could have less resistance to spin entry in the normal category (less restricted aft CG, more weight), because it can generate a higher AOA [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

final_quiz.q: A private pilot who is not training for any certificate or rating asks for a one-flight spin ride in your spin-approved trainer, as your passenger. What does 14 CFR 91.307 require?
options: Nothing, because 91.307(d) exempts any maneuver flown with a CFI on board
Only the passenger wears a parachute, since the CFI is a crewmember and exempt
Each occupant wears an approved parachute, since (d) covers only required spins
Parachutes only if neither pilot is a CFI or an ATP instructing under 61.67
final_quiz.why: 91.307(d)(2) lifts paragraph (c) only for spins and other maneuvers required by the regulations for a certificate or rating, given by a CFI or an ATP instructing under 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(d)]]. This ride is not required, so (c) applies: carrying a person who is not a crewmember, no maneuver past 60 degrees of bank or 30 degrees of pitch unless each occupant, you included, wears an approved parachute [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(c)]]. Application: a spin's nose-down attitude goes past 30 degrees.

final_quiz.q: Before the ground lesson, your applicant says she is terrified of spins. What does the AIH say about starting the spin lesson right away?
options: Go ahead: the facts in the lesson will replace the fear on their own
Postpone all spin topics until after her CFI practical test
Her fear may overwhelm her listening, so allay the anxiety first
Go ahead, but skip the sensations so she does not get more worried
final_quiz.why: A learner terrified of spins who tries to listen to a spin lesson may be overwhelmed by the emotion, so the anxiety and fear need to be allayed first [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]; treat fears as normal and describe the sensations and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].

final_quiz.q: Why does the AFH warn instructors about how they deliver stall, spin and upset training?
options: Spin training is mostly for entertainment, so it should be kept brief
Poorly delivered training often causes negative learning that stays with the pilot
Only an aerobatic instructor may legally give spin training in any airplane
Spins teach nothing useful unless they go past six full turns each time
final_quiz.why: Improper delivery of stall, spin and upset recovery training often results in negative learning, with severe consequences during training and later, when the pilot carries passengers [[24:113|AFH 5-8]].

final_quiz.q: Your applicant asks why she must practice incipient spins when she plans never to let a student spin. What purpose does AC 61-67C give?
options: To meet the 61.183(i) rule, which names incipient spins as a separate item
To train her to recover from a student's poorly performed stall or unusual attitude
To show the student how a flat spin develops from an aft CG loading
To prove the airplane is approved for spins before full spins are flown
final_quiz.why: Incipient spins are practiced to train the instructor applicant to recover from a student's poorly performed stall or unusual attitude that could lead to a spin [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300d]].

final_quiz.q: Your applicant failed her CFI practical test for deficiencies in spin instruction. What does she need before the retest?
options: Only a fresh 61.183(i) endorsement, which the examiner then accepts instead of flying
Nothing new; she may retest the next day in any airplane in the airplane category
A logbook record of three more spins, certified by any flight instructor
More training and an endorsement, a spin-certificated airplane, and a demonstration
final_quiz.why: She needs the additional training and an endorsement, must bring an aircraft certificated for spins, and must demonstrate instructional proficiency to the examiner [[60:227|14 CFR 61.49(b)]]; the endorsement cannot replace the test on a retest for spin deficiencies [[60:340|14 CFR 61.183(i)(2)]].

final_quiz.q: The evaluator, as your learner, applies full spin rudder about 10 knots above the stall, before the airplane has stalled. Which listed error is this, and what is the fix?
options: Ailerons not neutral on the entry; hold them neutral during the spin
Too little forward elevator; push the stick ahead of neutral now
Too little rudder on entry; push the pedal harder until it rotates
Not fully stalled before the spin input; raise the nose to a stall first
final_quiz.why: Failure to achieve a fully stalled condition before spin entry is a listed error [[24:131|AFH 5-26]]; the entry raises the nose to a pitch attitude that ensures a stall before the full rudder goes in [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

final_quiz.q: On her first spin training flight, your applicant has never stalled this trainer. What do the AFH and AC 61-67C suggest you do first?
options: Practice power-on and power-off stalls to learn this airplane's stall
Start with incipient spins only, recovering by 1,500 ft AGL
Start with a fully developed spin, so she sees the worst case early on
Start with spiral dives, which are easier to recover from than spins
final_quiz.why: Spin training may begin with power-on and power-off stalls in a clean configuration to learn the airplane's stall and recovery characteristics [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]].

final_quiz.q: You are clearing for a spin in a low-wing trainer. Which technique fits the AIM and the AFH?
options: Clear above and below while slowing, lowering a wing to look below
Clear once on reaching altitude, then look inside during the slow-down
Clear only ahead and above, since the spin will not move you sideways
Ask ATC for traffic, which replaces your own visual clearing
final_quiz.why: Clear above and below before any intentional spin, which may be done while slowing [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]; in a low-wing airplane, lower the wing in the direction of the turn and look [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

takeaways: A spin needs a stall plus yaw; take away either and there is no spin.
Find spin approval in the TCDS, the AFM/POH limitations or a placard, and check the day's weight and CG against it.
Plan the entry: terrain plus 4,000 ft plus about 1,000 ft for the first turn and 500 for each later one.
The turn indicator shows the spin direction; the ball does not. Rising airspeed means a spiral, not a spin.
Recover by the POH; without one: idle, ailerons neutral, full opposite rudder, brisk forward elevator, rudder neutral, ease out.
61.183(i) requires spin training and an endorsement; required CFI spin training needs no parachutes.
Teach in building blocks, brief the take-over, and expect anxiety, startle and airsickness.
cfi_notes: Three altitude numbers: the AFH says complete recovery at or above 1,500 ft AGL [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], AC 61-67C says practice from above 3,500 ft AGL [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]], and the CFI ACS says complete the Task no lower than 4,000 ft AGL (AI.X.I.S2). Plan your training to the ACS figure plus your planned turns.

Elevator timing differs: the AFH says apply forward elevator immediately after the rudder and not to wait for the rotation to stop [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]; AC 61-67C (2000) says move it forward when the rotation slows [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. Teach the POH first, then the newer AFH template.

Altitude loss figures differ: the AFH text gives about 1,000 ft for the first turn and half that for each later turn, while its Figure 5-16 and AC 61-67C give about 500 ft per 3-second turn [[24:128|AFH 5-23]] [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]. Plan with the larger first-turn figure.

Incipient phase length: the AFH text says two to four turns for most airplanes [[24:129|AFH 5-24]]; its Figure 5-16 says about 2 turns and 4 to 6 seconds in light aircraft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]]. Either way, start the incipient recovery before 360 degrees.

Airspeed in a spin: the AFH says low and constant [[24:130|AFH 5-25]], the PHAK says usually within 2 knots of the unaccelerated stall speed [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]], and AC 61-67C says it normally stabilizes below stall speed [[13:20|AC 61-67C 300f]]. All agree a rising airspeed is not a spin.

AC 61-67C chapter 4 describes spin rules by category under the older Part 23 (23.221 and the 23.1567 placards) [[13:21|AC 61-67C 400]]. The current rule is the performance-based 14 CFR 23.2150 [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]], and the AFH notes that 23.221(a) still applies to airplanes certified under it [[24:130|AFH 5-25]]. For any airplane, the TCDS, AFM and placards decide.

AC 61-67C paragraph 301 quotes 91.307(d) as covering an ATP instructing under 61.167 [[13:20|AC 61-67C 301]]; the current 14 CFR 91.307(d)(2)(ii) says 61.67 [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]]. Teach the CFR text.
No source in this set uses the memory aid 'PARE'. Teach the AFH's own six steps or your POH's wording; if you use a memory aid, make sure it matches the POH order.

The CFI ACS note lets the evaluator accept a certified logbook record instead of this Task, and 61.183(i)(2) lets an examiner accept the endorsement, except on a retest for spin deficiencies [[60:340|14 CFR 61.183(i)(2)]]. Bring the endorsement, but be ready to fly it.
gaps: The sources do not list which trainer models are approved for spins or their spin weight and CG limits; that comes only from each airplane's TCDS, AFM/POH and placards.
No source says how many spins or how many hours of spin training are enough for the 61.183(i) endorsement; AC 61-67C gives only the content. Use your judgment and syllabus.
None of the sources gives the altitude your particular airplane loses in a one-turn spin and pull-out. Measure it at a safe altitude and plan with it.
The sources give no standard words for briefing a spin or a set take-over point; write your own and use them every time.
The sources are silent on using an outside landmark to count turns or hold orientation in a spin; any such technique is instructor practice, not FAA guidance.

activities.title: True or false: the CFI spin rules
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A CFI applicant who first seeks a multiengine flight instructor rating still needs the spin training endorsement.
cards.why: True. AC 61-65K says the endorsement is required even when the applicant first seeks a flight instructor certificate with an airplane multiengine rating [[12:21|AC 61-65K 26.1]].

cards.s: With a valid 61.183(i) endorsement, the examiner must still always watch you spin.
cards.why: False. An examiner may accept the endorsement as evidence, unless it is a retest for spin deficiencies [[60:340|14 CFR 61.183(i)(2)]].

cards.s: AC 61-67C says spin avoidance, incipient spins and spins should be practiced from an altitude above 3,500 ft AGL.
cards.why: True. AC 61-67C 300b gives above 3,500 ft AGL [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300b]]; on the CFI checkride the Task must be completed no lower than 4,000 ft AGL (AI.X.I.S2).

cards.s: A nylon parachute carried for emergency use must have been packed within the preceding 180 days.
cards.why: True. Synthetic-fiber parachutes: 180 days; any natural fiber: 60 days [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(a)]].

cards.s: In required CFI spin training, the applicant may go without a parachute but the instructor must wear one.
cards.why: False. Neither the person receiving the instruction nor the instructor giving it must wear one [[13:20|AC 61-67C 301b]].

cards.s: The endorsement is made by the flight instructor who provided the spin training.
cards.why: True. The logbook or training record should be endorsed by the instructor who provided the training [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300]]; AC 61-65K has a sample [[12:49|AC 61-65K A.49]].

activities.title: Spin altitude numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You level at 6,800 ft MSL. Highest terrain is 1,500 ft MSL. Using the AFH loss figures and ignoring the recovery, how many full turns can you spin before reaching the CFI ACS floor?
items.why: Room: 6,800 - 1,500 - 4,000 = 1,300 ft (AI.X.I.S2). One turn loses about 1,000 ft; two turns lose 1,000 + 500 = 1,500 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], more than 1,300. So 1 turn.

items.q: Using AC 61-67C's rough estimate of altitude loss per turn, about what is the descent rate in a spin, in feet per minute?
items.why: About 500 ft per 3-second turn [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]: 500 / 3 x 60 = 10,000 ft per minute.

items.q: With the same 3-second turn, what is the rotation rate in degrees per second?
items.why: One turn is 360 degrees in about 3 seconds [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]]: 360 / 3 = 120 degrees per second, 40 times a standard-rate turn of 3 degrees per second [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]].

items.q: Your 1,600 lb trainer pulls out of a spin at about 2.5 G. How much lift are the wings producing?
items.why: Load factor is the ratio of wing lift to airplane weight [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]], and a proper spin recovery is about 2.5 G [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]: 1,600 x 2.5 = 4,000 lb.

items.q: An older emergency parachute with a silk canopy was packed 45 days ago. For how many more days may it be carried?
items.why: A parachute with any part made of silk or another natural fiber must have been packed within the preceding 60 days [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307(a)]]: 60 - 45 = 15 days.

activities.title: Your first spin student
activities.intro: You are a new CFI giving a commercial pilot the spin training 61.183(i) requires, in a trainer whose POH approves spins in the utility category. Highest terrain in the practice area is 1,000 ft MSL.

steps.s: Weight and balance shows you inside the normal category envelope but over the utility category maximum weight with full fuel. What do you do?
options: Go, and simply add more altitude to the entry to cover the extra weight
Go, but limit each spin to one turn so the overweight does not matter
Go: the CG is inside the envelope, which is what matters for spins
Reduce the fuel or load until you are within the utility limits
steps.why: Spins are approved only within the AFM/POH limits, and loaded in the normal category the airplane may not recover from a spin beyond one turn [[24:130|AFH 5-25]] [[24:131|AFH 5-26]].

steps.s: In the brief she asks how far you will let her go if her recovery is wrong. What do you set?
options: No limit: let her find her own way out of the spin, however long that takes
A plan to stay on the controls with her and push against her inputs if she freezes up in the spin
A limit you will decide in the air, depending on how calm she looks at the time
A take-over point set now, such as one turn, and the words you will use to take over
steps.why: Learners should never exceed the instructor's limits, and anxious learners can be very strong, so take the controls with 'I have the flight controls' rather than fight [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. Letting a learner go part way into a mistake is only 'safety permitting' [[25:182|AIH 9-12]], and the AC plan recovers no later than one full turn [[13:19|AC 61-67C 300e]].

steps.s: You plan up to a two-turn spin. What is the lowest entry altitude that still meets the CFI ACS standard, using the AFH loss figures?
options: 6,500 ft MSL
5,000 ft MSL
6,000 ft MSL
2,500 ft MSL
steps.why: Floor 1,000 + 4,000 = 5,000 ft MSL (AI.X.I.S2). Two turns lose about 1,000 + 500 = 1,500 ft [[24:128|AFH 5-23]], so enter at 6,500 ft MSL or higher.

steps.s: In an incipient spin she calls 'left spin!' because the ball is pegged left, but the turn coordinator's airplane is banked right. What do you tell her?
options: Trust the ball; it is the most direct sign of which way the airplane yaws
It is not a spin; a pegged ball always means a skid, so add rudder
It is a right spin: the turn indicator shows the direction, the ball does not
Look at the heading indicator, which is the most reliable sign of spin direction
steps.why: The turn indicator shows the spin direction; the ball moves according to where it is mounted, not the spin direction [[24:129|AFH 5-24]].

steps.s: After the rotation stops she keeps full left rudder in as the airspeed builds. What is the risk, and what do you say?
options: None: holding rudder until level flight keeps the airplane coordinated as speed builds
Yaw or sideslip, possibly a spin the other way: rudder neutral now
A secondary spin to the left; she should add more power to fly out of it
A stall from too much forward elevator; ease back on the stick right now
steps.why: Neutralize the rudder after rotation stops; otherwise the increasing airspeed causes yaw or sideslip [[24:130|AFH 5-25]], possibly a secondary spin [[24:131|AFH 5-26]], or a spin in the opposite direction [[13:13|AC 61-67C 111]].
